div.head: Disputation 1
On the Object of This Doctrine and the Various Meanings of Faith
div.p: DISPUTATION I: INTRODUCTORY. ON THE OBJECT OF THIS DOCTRINE AND THE VARIOUS MEANINGS OF FAITH.

For the clarity and understanding of any doctrine, two things are especially necessary. One is to have prior knowledge of the object whose knowledge is intended, for it is as it were the end and goal of the whole doctrine. The other is to distinguish terms and to remove their ambiguity, lest on account of their equivocation the disputation be obscure and ineffective. These two things, therefore, must be accomplished in the present disputation; for we have proposed to treat of Faith; but the word faith, in the common opinion of all, is usually taken in various ways, and therefore it is necessary first to distinguish its meanings, and from these to conclude and, as it were, to separate the proper object with which the present doctrine is concerned.

div.head: Section 1
In What Ways Faith Is Properly and Catholically Taken
div.p: SECTION I. In What Ways Faith Is Properly and Catholically Taken.

2. First assertion, bipartite: that faith pertains to both the will and the intellect. — The prior part is certain. — Budé and Valla have doubts about the latter. — It is established nonetheless first from the usage of the Latins. — Second, from the Philosophers. — Third, from the Fathers. — Fourth, from Scripture. — Fifth, from reason. — I say, therefore, first that the word faith, taken in its fullest proper sense, sometimes signifies a perfection of the will, and sometimes of the intellect. Concerning the prior part, neither heretics nor Catholics have doubts, and therefore I pass over it, to be proved and explained more fully in the following assertion; but concerning the latter part, some even Catholic authors have doubts, at least insofar as the Latin propriety of the word is concerned; for Budé, in his Annotations on the Pandects, book 1, on the Corrupted Slave, together with Lorenzo Valla, book 5 of the Elegantiae, ch. 30, considers that this word does not properly signify the persuasion of the intellect, or assent, but that it has been adapted by the faithful for signifying this.
Nonetheless, the proposed part is certain — first, from the usage of the Latins; for Cicero, in book 2 of the Divinations, said that faith should not be given to the vices of the insane — that is, assent, credence; hence Virgil, in Aeneid 4: I believe indeed (nor is the faith vain) that the race of Gods exists. And to have faith in someone, among approved Latin authors, is the same as to assent to what he says, as may be seen from Terence and others in Calepino, s.v. Faith.
Second, the Philosophers too, together with Boethius, define an argument as a speech that produces faith in a doubtful matter; and in Aristotle, Problems, sect. 18, q. 3, we read that faith produced by testimony is very easily acquired; but testimony produces assent and credence.
Third, this usage of the word is most frequent among the Fathers; Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter, ch. 31, expressly posits the distinction of a twofold faith: one is that by which we faithfully promise something to another; the other is that by which we believe one who speaks; he holds the same in the book On Lying, c. 20, and Letter 19 to Jerome. Likewise Isidore, Etymologies, book 8, ch. 2; Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 45, when he says that faith has no demonstration; Chrysostom and other commentators commonly, on Hebrews 11, and in other scriptural passages to be cited shortly.
Fourth, and what concerns us most, this is the frequent usage of Scripture, even when speaking of justifying faith, whatever the heretics may contend; this is clear from Paul, Hebrews 11, for after having said at the end of chapter 10: The just man lives by faith, he adds at the beginning of chapter 11: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen, which description we shall examine more fully in its proper place; for now, that particle — evidence (argumentum) — is most to the point, for it openly signifies an act of the intellect, just as the Greek word elegxos, which the Greek Fathers expound, means conviction and firm assent. Then St. Paul adds: By faith we understand that the ages were made by the word of God; therefore faith pertains to the intellect. Finally he adds: Without faith it is impossible to please God, and gives the reason, namely: He who comes to God must believe that he exists, which does not pertain to the will, as is self-evident. There is also the excellent testimony of Romans 4, where Paul says of Abraham: He was fully strengthened in faith, knowing that he who promised is also able to bring it about; but to know or to understand is an act of the intellect, and he speaks of the faith by which Abraham was justified, and plainly speaks of the same faith in the same sense throughout that epistle; hence in 2 Corinthians 5, he opposes faith to sight, saying: We walk by faith and not by sight; and in chapter 10, on account of faith he says that the intellect is brought into captivity in obedience to Christ; and in 1 Corinthians 13, because of faith he says: We know in part, etc. And finally, Christ the Lord, in Matthew 9, when he had asked some who were seeking healing: Do you believe that I am able to do this for you? and they had answered affirmatively, he adds: According to your faith, be it done to you. Other passages I have cited in book 8 on Grace, ch. 15, n. 2.
Hence the following argument is concluded: to believe something to be true, or to be possible, or simply to be, is the function of the intellect; but this is the function of faith, as is clear from the testimonies cited; therefore.

4. The aforesaid meaning is extended to truthfulness. — It is likewise extended to its object, and to the obligation of embracing that same truthfulness, and to conscience, and to the faith of legal instruments. — From this meaning the word has been derived to signify other things, on account of the affinity or analogy that other authors number among the various meanings of this word; and they can conveniently be referred back to it. For in the first place the word has been derived to signify truthfulness, which is also a moral virtue, because it is either not distinct from fidelity (fidelitate), or is very closely akin to it, as is gathered from St. Thomas, II-II, q. 109, together with the notes of Cajetan, q. 113, at the beginning; and Antoninus, Part 4, tit. 5, ch. 16.
And so Paul, in the aforesaid passage of Romans 3, in order to prove that the faith of God is not made void, says: God is truthful; and in Apocalypse 19, Christ is called a faithful witness — that is, truthful. And from this the word is further extended to signify the object of fidelity, or truthfulness, and so it is said to signify the promise itself, insofar as it ought to be made with faithful intent and afterwards fulfilled; and in this way many understand the words cited: They made void their first faith. And in the same way faith is commonly attributed to words themselves insofar as in them there is objective truthfulness with respect to the moral virtue of truthfulness. So it is said in Jeremiah 7: Faith has perished and is not found in their mouth. Furthermore, because in the right performance of any duty there is found a certain moral obligation and a kind of implicit agreement, therefore one who fulfills his duty is commonly called faithful, which is frequent in the Gospel: Matthew 25 and Luke 19: Well done, good and faithful servant; 1 Corinthians 4: Here now it is required among stewards that a man be found faithful. Finally, because the proximate obligation of acting rightly arises from conscience, conscience too is commonly signified by the name faith: Romans 14: Whatever is not of faith is sin — that is, what is not according to conscience, although this derivation can also be understood from another angle, as I shall say shortly. Faith is also commonly attributed to public legal instruments, such as the titles in law regarding the Faith of Instruments, insofar as in them there is morally certain truth and consequently sufficient authority for proving the truth; all of which pertains to that first meaning of this word that belongs to the will.

5. Regarding the meaning of trust (fiducia), some agree. — Concerning the other meaning pertaining to trust (fiduciae), there is a controversy not to be dismissed on account of the heretics of this time, who abuse this meaning and want the name of faith in Sacred Scripture — wherever it speaks of justifying faith — to be understood in that sense. Many Catholics, however, although they differ from the heretics on this point, think that faith is often taken in Scripture in the sense of trust (fiduciam): this is the view of Vega above, and in book 9 on the Council of Trent, ch. 28; and Casale, On Fourfold Justice, part 1, book 2, ch. 5; and Jansen in the Concordia, chs. 30, 32 and 35; and modern commentators on St. Thomas II-II, at the beginning. They principally adduce that text of James 1: Let him ask in faith, nothing doubting — because Catholic faith does not have as its object the obtaining of a prayer, such that one could be certain it would come about; therefore it cannot be in this sense that a praying believer is asked not to waver in faith; therefore the meaning must be that he should not waver in trust (fiducia). In the same way Luke 17 seems to be understood: If you have faith, etc. — for it cannot be understood of belief, both for the same reason and because not everyone who believes obtains a miracle, but only one who has a special trust (fiduciam). And the rebuke of Christ in Matthew 14 also seems to be understood in this sense: O you of little faith, why did you doubt — for it cannot be understood of doubt in the assent of divine faith, because that doubt destroys faith entirely; so someone doubting in that way would not be called of little faith but of no faith, a plain unbeliever. It is therefore understood of wavering in trust (fiducia), a sign of which is also this: that the doubt arose from fear — for, as it says there, when Peter saw the strong wind, he was afraid; but fear is opposed to trust (fiduciae), as St. Thomas (to be cited shortly) teaches. Added to this is the fact that in Latin usage, as Calepino attests, faith is also taken in the sense of trust (fiducia), where he cites Cicero, in the Pro Quinto Ligario, saying: Note with what faithfulness I defend his cause, who betray my own — and similar examples.

6. Others reject it — and their view is more appealing. — Trust (fiducia) is distinguished from Catholic faith. — Nonetheless, other theologians do not admit this meaning of faith, at least as a usage of Scripture. This is the position of Soto, book 2 on Nature and Grace, ch. 6; and Horantius, On Catholic Loci, book one, ch. 64; and it is defended at length by Bellarmine, book one on Justification, ch. 11. Their opinion, although perhaps not strictly necessary, seems to me nonetheless very pious and probable, better suited to confuting the heretics, and simpler to speak with — or, as I would put it, more unambiguous in this matter. To explain that position: I presuppose first, as regards the matter itself, that trust (fiducia) is in reality something distinct from Catholic or justifying faith. This is plainly gathered from the Council of Trent, session 6, ch. 8, together with canons 9, 12 and 13, where it condemns those who say that trust (fiducia) alone justifies, and places faith as the first foundation of justification. Then there is the excellent testimony of Paul, 1 Timothy 3: Those who have ministered well will acquire a good standing for themselves, and confidence (fiduciam) in faith. Therefore trust (fiducia) is not faith, for he would not have rightly said: And confidence (fiduciam) in faith. And Ephesians 3, he says that confidence (fiducia) in Christ is had or acquired through faith; therefore it is distinct from faith.

7. Trust (fiducia) is strengthened hope. — Next it must be added that trust (fiduciam), as it is distinguished from faith, is nothing other than hope, connoting a certain perfection or strength of it.
This can be gathered from Job chapter 8: The hope of the hypocrite shall perish, and his trust (fiducia) is like a spider's web; the latter words explain the former. Hence St. Thomas, in Book 3, dist. 26, q. 1, art. 3, ad 5, said that hope in good things is called trust (fiduciam); which he explains more fully in I-II, q. 40, art. 2, ad 2, saying that trust (fiduciam) is derived from faith, but is nonetheless hope, as it were strengthened by its conjunction with faith. And still better in II-II, q. 129, art. 6, ad 2, and it is plainly gathered from Paul in the passages cited; for on this account he calls for trust (fiduciam) in faith, or through faith. Hence, in Romans 4, he says of Abraham: he believed in hope against hope, because out of perfect faith he conceived hope concerning the promised son, against the hope that nature did not promise; hence he adds: he did not weaken in distrust (diffidentia); and further: he did not waver in distrust (diffidentia), but was strengthened in faith; that firm hope, therefore, was trust (fiducia), which is the contrary of distrust (diffidentiae). He adds moreover that he did not weaken in faith, because he did not consider his own body as dead, but rather the power and word of God. Trust (fiducia) is therefore a perfection of the will, whose hope is founded in faith.

8. Faith in Scripture Is Not Taken for Trust (fiducia), Except Perhaps by Taking the Cause for the Effect. — From these things, therefore, I conclude that, although the former opinion can be defended with probability, by saying that the name of a cause is sometimes transferred to signify the effect, and so the name of faith can sometimes signify the trust (fiduciam) of the will, insofar as it receives its perfection from faith, nevertheless this analogy is not necessary for us, nor do the passages of Scripture cited above compel us to admit that signification. For first, as regards the faith of prayer, of which James speaks, it is certain that some true and Catholic faith is required for the efficacy of prayer. For, as Paul said, Romans 10: How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Hence what James says: Let him ask in faith without wavering, can first be understood of the wavering that is opposed to the truth of divine faith; not because it is necessary for each person to believe absolutely that his prayer will have its effect, but only conditionally, if it has all the necessary conditions under which the promise of prayer was made, so that he does not waver concerning that promise: Whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you shall receive it, which is to be understood in that sense. Or secondly, if we wish James to be speaking of non-wavering in the very affect of praying, he therefore said that one asking in faith should not waver at all,
not because that faith is trust (fiducia), but because it is the root of trust (fiduciae), and because from perfect consideration of faith, and of the goodness and benevolence of God, which faith teaches, it comes about that the faithful person prays with firm affect and without wavering; just as Peter, 1 Peter, ch. 5, said: Resist him, strong in faith. Not because resistance to temptation formally occurs through faith — for it occurs through the will aided by grace — but because faith is what moves and directs the will. And so also in our present case, Paul said that Abraham, confirmed in faith, did not waver in distrust (diffidentia). And in another place he advises to have trust (fiduciam) in faith, that is, founded in faith. And for the same reason, when Christ rebuked Peter for being of little faith, and similarly the other Apostles, he speaks of true faith; and he did not rebuke them because they doubted the truth of faith or revelation, but because they had a weak faith and did not rightly use it to consider those things that could raise up the affect and trust (fiduciam). And in this way I have explained this faith of prayer more extensively in Book 1, On Prayer, ch. 24, and it is very consistent with the teaching of St. Thomas, II-II, in the passage cited, and it seems to me to be the opinion of Jerome in the Dialogue against the Luciferians, somewhat past the middle, whatever Marianus Victor may say there in the scholium. For Jerome does not expound those passages concerning trust (fiducia), but concerning faith, whether living or efficaciously working, and considering the truth of faith. And the same thing is to be said proportionally concerning the faith of miracles, of which Jerome also speaks there; but concerning this faith something must be said specifically in the course of the material. And therefore in the present I do not explain it further.

9. Third Assertion: Faith, Even as Related to the Intellect, Has Various Meanings. — Third, it must be principally said that the name of faith, even as related to the intellect, has multiple meanings, partly equivocal or analogical, partly under some common notion; which it is necessary to explain briefly for the use of the word in this matter, and for establishing its object.
First, therefore, any assent of the intellect determined toward one part is customarily called faith, which is common among all. And in this way can be understood that saying of Augustine, On the Predestination of the Saints, ch. 29: To believe is to think with assent. For to believe is the same as to give faith. And in the same way many understand the common description of an argument, that it is a discourse about a doubtful matter that produces credence, which some extend even to demonstration. Indeed, Hales, Bonaventure, and Gabriel, cited above, think that even intuitive knowledge and even a clear vision of God is sometimes called faith, so understanding that passage of
Romans 1: The justice of God in it, that is, in the Gospel, is revealed from faith to faith, that is, from obscure faith to clear vision — which was Bede's exposition of that passage; but this does not seem right to me, because it is not the mind of Paul there; for he is not dealing with vision, but with proper faith in the coming Christ; and this is what he says: From faith to faith. As Toletus, Benedict Pererius, and others declare from the common opinion of the Fathers there. Likewise it does not accord with other passages of Paul, in which he opposes faith to vision: We walk by faith and not by sight. Hence I do not believe that the vision of God is anywhere called faith in Scripture; indeed not even in common speech is any intuitive vision called by the name of faith. Wherefore, if this word is extended to evident knowledge, it is only to abstractive knowledge, and that which is had through discourse; more frequently however, and less improperly, it is said of any opinative assent, either because it is fearful, or obscure, or because it regularly includes authority. Hence Aristotle, De Anima 3, ch. 3, text 157, said: Faith follows opinion. And St. Thomas, II-II, q. 129, art. 6, said that a vehement opinion is called faith.

10. From this meaning two others could be derived, which I have touched on above. — One is that by which faith is said of conscience. For conscience is an act of the intellect, as St. Thomas teaches, I, q. 79 and I-II, q. 19, art. 5, and it consists in a certain firm practical judgment about things to be done; which judgment regularly rests on conjectures and authority; and therefore it could be called faith, and can be called by us practical faith, according to which a person is said to be of good or bad faith, which is very commonly used in law. The other meaning was that in which faith is attributed to instruments and public documents and the like, according to the legal titles on the credibility of instruments. For because such instruments are apt to generate faith in the mind, or assent, they are therefore called faithful (fidelia); just as a medicine apt to generate health is called healthful (sana).

11. The Most Important Meaning of Faith Is for Obscure Knowledge Founded on the Testimony of a Speaker, Which Is Divided into Divine and Human. — Now indeed in common usage, the word faith has been contracted to signify obscure knowledge founded on the testimony of a speaker, and this is the sense which serves the present purpose. But further, this faith must be distinguished into divine and human, which two members, although they are not equivocal as the preceding ones are (for they can have a common notion, perhaps univocal — about which elsewhere),
nonetheless differ essentially by reason of the formal objects on which they are founded; for divine faith is founded on the testimony of God (as we shall see), while human faith is founded on human, or created, authority — if we wish to include under this member the faith that can be given to an angel speaking in his own name, or by his proper authority. In the present, therefore, we omit human faith, which pertains to the Philosophers, and we treat of supernatural and divine faith. In the supernatural order, moreover, there is also a multiple use of this word, even as pertaining to the intellect, which I shall explain better in the following section.

div.head: Section 2
Which Supernatural Faith Is the Proper Object of This Matter, and in What Order It Is to Be Treated
div.p: SECTION II. Which Supernatural Faith Is the Proper Object of This Matter, and in What Order It Is to Be Treated.

2. Although We Must Treat of Divine Faith, the Declaration of Human Faith or That Common to Both Still Serves. — Next it must be established that the object of the present doctrine is not human faith, nor the notion of faith common to human and divine alone, but divine faith according to its proper notion; for that alone is a theological virtue and the foundation of salvation,
and tends toward God as a supernatural end, for which reasons it is considered above all in Theology; but because the proper notion of this faith presupposes the common one, and because, generally speaking, it is not obtained without some ministry and as it were the assistance of human faith, Theology cannot therefore abstract entirely from considering these notions; not however as parts of its proper object, but either by presupposing them or by explaining them insofar as is necessary for itself.

3. Divine Faith Includes Three Things. — A Question: Which of These Three Is the Matter of This Treatise. — It must further be considered that divine faith intrinsically includes three things: the habit or light of faith, its act, and its object; and these three, even taken individually, are customarily signified in Scripture by the name of faith. For the doctrine, or object of faith, is understood that passage of Gal. 1: When faith had come, etc., and ch. 3: from the hearing of faith; and Eph. 4: One God, one faith; and Apoc. 2: You have not denied my faith; and so also said Athanasius, in the Creed: This is the Catholic faith, which unless one believes firmly and faithfully — for the faith that is believed is the object of the virtue of faith. For the act, that passage of Matthew 9 is understood: According to your faith be it done to you; and that of Rom. 1: Your faith is proclaimed in the whole world; and in the whole eleventh chapter of Hebrews, faith is taken in the same way when those various effects are attributed to it; and whenever Scripture commands faith as necessary for salvation, that faith is what is spoken of, since precepts are given concerning acts. For the habit of faith, that passage of 1 Cor. 13 is rightly understood: Now there remain these three: faith, etc.; and in the same sense speaks the Council of Trent, session six, chapter seven, when it says that in justification faith, hope, and charity are infused simultaneously. And beyond these meanings, we find three others in Scripture pertaining also to faith of the supernatural order: namely, insofar as faith is required for miracles (which is called the faith of miracles or signs), and insofar as a certain faith is placed among the freely given graces, and another among the fruits of the Holy Spirit. It can therefore be asked whether faith, as it encompasses all these things, is the proper object of this doctrine, or under which notion. On this it must be said briefly that all these things are indeed explained in this matter; yet, by the common consensus and mind of the Theologians, the habit or light of faith itself is the proper object of this doctrine. For the matter or object believed is called faith through faith only by reason of the habit or act of faith itself, and is thus considered only insofar as it can terminate the relation of faith to itself; but the habit and act, although they are considered per se and principally, nevertheless the habit is as it were a permanent form and the principle of the act itself, and is therefore posited as the chief object of the whole doctrine; the rest are considered as annexed to faith itself.

4. A Small Question That Arises. — It Is Resolved. — But someone will ask: since the light of faith is the first principle and foundation of the whole of Theology and all its parts, how can it be the object of some part of that same Theology? For the notion of object has the notion of a term; but the same thing cannot be both principle and term with respect to the same thing, since these denote contrary relations. Also, because otherwise either the principle would be begged in the course of such a doctrine, or it would be necessary to resolve it into some higher principle. Nevertheless this is easily resolved and understood by considering that intellectual light is reflexive upon itself; for the intellect is the principle of knowing itself, and the light of glory is also the principle of seeing itself, and so in these cases the notions of principle and term do not conflict, because they are distinguished by reason and denomination alone. Thus, therefore, the light of faith is the principle of believing itself; for by the same faith we believe that faith is infused in us, and that it is supernatural, and other such things. And so it comes about that Theology can reason from believed principles about faith itself, and gather other properties belonging to that same faith without begging the question, and without resolution into a higher principle; and in this way faith can be a part of the object of faith.
